name: Weight loss for chin definition

card.summary: Losing body fat to reveal the chin and jawline; plausible where fullness is soft tissue, but no studies test it and bone structure is not changed.
card.note: Wikipedia notes a double-chin look can also come from bone structure, not fat.

quick.overview:
Weight loss for chin definition is the idea that lowering overall body fat reduces fullness under the chin and makes the jawline look sharper.

Wikipedia describes a double chin as arising either from soft-tissue fat or from jaw bones that do not project far enough; no study found here tests weight loss for chin appearance.
quick.mechanism: Reducing overall body fat shrinks fat cells, including those under the chin. The sources reviewed do not address whether fat loss can be targeted to one area.
quick.risks: The sources reviewed list no risks specific to this approach. When the cause is bone structure, fat loss is not described as changing the chin's projection.

lead: Weight loss for chin definition is the approach of reducing overall body fat so that the area under the chin and along the jaw looks leaner and the chin and jawline stand out more. People use it to reduce a soft, rounded under-chin fold, often called a double chin, and to make the jaw outline sharper in photos and in person.[1]

Wikipedia describes two different causes of a double-chin look: in some overweight people, fat beneath the chin forms a fold, while in others, often of normal weight, the jaw bones do not project far enough forward so that the chin appears to blend into the neck.[1] Weight loss is relevant to the first type, and surgery such as genioplasty or jaw advancement is described for the second.[1][3]

Researchers at the University of Toronto digitally altered face photos and reported that a BMI change of about 1.33 kg/m2 was needed before people noticed a change in facial weight, and roughly twice that before faces looked more attractive.[4] A small study of gastric-bypass patients found modestly higher attractiveness ratings after about 20 percent weight loss.[5]

chain: Less subcutaneous fat under the chin and along the jaw
angle.text: People cut body fat through diet and exercise so that fullness under the chin and cheeks decreases and the jaw outline shows. Where the underlying bone is the limiting factor, individuals commonly combine fat loss with other approaches.

paras: According to Wikipedia, the soft-tissue form is attributed to excess subcutaneous fat around the neck, whereas the bone form occurs in people of normal weight when the jaw bones are insufficiently projecting.[1] Subcutaneous fat is distributed unevenly through the body, with the number of fat cells varying by region and their size changing with nutritional state.[2] Because of this, how much leanness shows in the face varies by person.

sections.h: How weight loss affects the face
paras: In the Toronto photo study by Nicholas Rule and Daniel Re, published in Social Psychological and Personality Science, participants compared digitally altered faces; a BMI change of about 1.33 was needed to notice a difference in weight, and a decrease of about 2.38 (women) or 2.59 (men) before faces looked more attractive, equal to roughly 6.3 kg or 8.2 kg for average-height people.[4] Rule said people need to lose about twice as much for others to find them more attractive.[4] Because the faces were digitally altered, the figures come from simulated faces rather than people who lost weight.[4]

Wikipedia lists surgical removal of the fat pad with a hyoid lift for the soft-tissue form and genioplasty or orthognathic surgery for bony deficiency.[1] Chin augmentation can be done by implants, sliding genioplasty or fillers.[3]

A 2015 Archives of Plastic Surgery study of 14 Roux-en-Y gastric bypass patients at Boston Medical Center, with mean weight loss of 20 percent, had online respondents rate before and after photos. Post-operative photos scored on average 0.256 points higher for attractiveness, while perceived age went up for six patients and down for five, and BMI change did not correlate significantly with either measure.[5] No study found tests lifestyle weight loss specifically for chin or jawline definition.
